audience.programmeDescription: Utrecht’s Philosophy bachelor studies questions about knowledge, reality, moral responsibility and political justice. Students develop philosophical arguments, read texts from different periods and choose an advanced package. This example follows Ethics and Politics.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR options share study of ethics and the philosophy of mind. They differ in their emphasis on historical interpretation, rights and public institutions, or cognition and AI. Utrecht offers a more extensive philosophy curriculum and requires a philosophy thesis.

cellNotes.text: UCR introduces ancient philosophical ideas alongside later debates. Utrecht provides a dedicated chronological study of ancient philosophy.
Utrecht follows the development of early modern philosophy through close reading of major thinkers.
Utrecht follows the history of philosophical thought from Kant onward.
Both courses examine major ethical theories and ask what makes actions right or wrong.
Both courses examine political power, freedom and justice. Utrecht also develops social philosophy through intensive writing.
Both courses examine the mind–body problem and competing accounts of consciousness and mental life.
Utrecht studies scepticism, what counts as knowledge and how to distinguish science from pseudoscience.
Both courses use formal logic to assess arguments. Utrecht also introduces questions about linguistic meaning.
This course alternates with History of Ethics. Utrecht lists History of Political Philosophy for academic years starting in an odd calendar year, which includes 2027–28.
Utrecht builds on introductory ethics to study rights, duties, consent and moral equality.
Utrecht asks whether moral claims can be objectively true and how moral knowledge is possible.
Utrecht studies global justice through political philosophy, including migration, trade and distribution of resources.
Utrecht studies philosophical accounts of art in a dedicated course.
Utrecht provides a dedicated course in continental philosophy.
Students complete at least 22.5 EC at level 3 before beginning the graduation sequence. The seminar prepares the thesis in the following block.
This example uses the 7.5 EC thesis. The 15 EC research project requires agreement with the programme coordinator and uses 7.5 EC of open elective space.
Choose a minor, a second Philosophy specialisation or approved study abroad. Across all 60 EC of elective space, at least 15 EC must be at level 2 or 3.
Choose electives, a second minor or an internship of up to 15 EC.

notes.text: UCR offers substantial study of ethics, political philosophy, the mind and agency. Utrecht devotes more of the degree to philosophy, including a chronological history sequence, advanced study in one philosophical area and a required philosophy thesis.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

DISARIN111.name: AI Ethics
DISARIN111.text: AI Ethics examines artificial intelligence from philosophical and psychological perspectives. Topics include fairness, privacy, responsibility, human-value alignment, moral status and political or existential risks. Students apply ethical frameworks to questions about human behaviour and interaction, synthesise research in an analytical psychology project, and produce a research-based podcast.

DISARIN212.name: Logic & Discrete Mathematics
DISARIN212.text: Introduces formal logic, abstract reasoning and proof. Students work with propositions, quantified statements, sets, Boolean algebra, functions and relations, direct and indirect proofs, induction and recursion. A final component models processes and games without chance and investigates winning strategies.

HCBCOGN312.name: Psycholinguistics
HCBCOGN312.text: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.

MCCHEAM315.name: Heritage & Ancient Democracy
MCCHEAM315.text:
In the modern world democracy is associated with participation, rationality and freedom. In this course, we go back to the roots of democracy in ancient Greece, when to a modern observer, it was not very democratic at all: foreigners, slaves and women were excluded from elections and political decision-making. Even so, the inclusion of all classes, also the poor, in politics was after antiquity not achieved until the mid-nineteenth century.


Ancient commentators criticised Athenian democracy for being too extreme just because of this broad inclusion. They argued that many were too uneducated, too emotional, and too irrational to see through the cheap play on emotions by demagogues and would-be tyrants.


This course investigates how Athenian democracy was built, how it was intertwined with myth and religion, and expressed in art, literature and architecture. It traces the loci of democracy in archaeology, and analyses its temporary collapse in the crisis of the late fifth century BC. Most importantly, we put ourselves in our socio-political ancestors’ shoes by engaging in a simulation of the Athenian assembly, in which we have to make decisions that will change our lives forever. In doing so, we use the ancient heritage of democracy for an experiment in applied sociology – to not only understand, but to feel the meaning of political decision-making.
